newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha, Socialists at impasse on new Albania govt.
newsitem.headline: Berisha, Socialists at impasse on new Albania govt.

text.p: Formation of a new government in Albania remained blocked on Sunday because of a standoff in which President Sali Berisha is withholding a decree that would convene parliament and the new Socialist majority is refusing to meet him.

Berisha, whose Democratic Party suffered a resounding defeat in parliamentary elections on June 29, has promised to resign once he has "fulfilled his constitutional obligations", but so far he has shown no sign of wishing to step down quickly.
He met leaders of his Democrats and smaller parties on Saturday to discuss when parliament should meet and who should be premier, but Socialist leaders said he no longer had the right to do so.
"We are not going to meet President Sali Berisha because his last act should be convening the parliament," Socialist Party organising secretary Namik Dokle told Reuters.
"It is not up to him to launch talks on the new government and it is absurd to ask the other parties which won less than two percent (of the vote) about the next prime minister."
Dokle said that, in the Socialists' view, Berisha was just one of the 155 deputies in parliament.
Berisha's Socialist party opponents and their coalition allies won a total of 117 seats, to the Democrats' 27.
The president has indicated that he would prefer the interim prime minister, Bashkim Fino, to stay on as head of government rather than Socialist leader Fatos Nano, the party's preferred candidate.
Nano threatened that, if Berisha refused to convene parliament, the assembly would meet without waiting for a presidential decree.
"He should observe the promise he made, namely to resign once the parliament is convened," Nano told the daily newspaper Gazeta Shqiptare.
He was quoted as saying that the Democratic Party's election defeat meant they no longer had any right to discuss the next government.

"We want to remind them we won two thirds of parliament and it's up to us to decide the future of the country...Berisha is a politician of the past, an old political factor, responsible for the destruction of the state," he added.
Berisha's government resigned in March at the height of unrest which followed the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid investment schemes. Much of the country is still ruled by armed gangs.

Diplomats who have urged a new government to get to work say they are concerned that there may be no prime minister to attend a donors' meeting in Rome at the end of July to discuss aid for the shattered country.
